title: Counting versus measuring
question: What makes a variable discrete rather than continuous?
hook: Some quantities leap from value to value with nothing in between, and that changes which maths you can use on them.
idea: A discrete variable has a gap around each permitted value, and its probabilities are described by mass functions rather than densities.

beats.prompt: A variable can be exactly 2 or exactly 3, and nothing in between. Is it continuous or discrete?

choices.label: Continuous, because 2 and 3 are real numbers
choices.feedback: Being a real number is not enough: a continuous variable needs possible values between any two of its values, and here there are none between 2 and 3.

choices.label: Discrete, because there is a gap on each side of each value
Continuous, because it has two end values to stop at
choices.feedback: Having end values does not make a variable continuous. What counts is whether values exist between any two permitted values.

beats.explain: There is a non-infinitesimal gap around each value with no permitted values, so it is discrete around those values.

beats.prompt: match each situation to the tool that goes with it
beats.explain: Each kind of variable, and each treatment of time, has its own matching description.

items: Any value in a range of the real numbers
beats.explain: Continuous variables can take any value in a range; discrete ones have separated permitted values such as integers.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: A variable can take only the values 0 and 1.
So there is a gap on each side of each value.
That makes it a discrete variable.
So calculus methods are the natural tool for it.
beats.explain: Calculus methods do not readily lend themselves to problems with discrete variables; they are often used for continuous ones.
